description: The problem involves a decision whose reversibility matters. Sunk costs, switching costs, or escalation dynamics are structurally present. The structural question is how much optionality is being consumed or preserved.
detect_when: Past investments create pressure to continue on the current path regardless of merit
Switching away from the current course would be costly or disruptive
The decision forecloses future options or locks in a trajectory
Escalation of commitment is a risk — the more invested, the harder to reverse
coverage_signals: The answer distinguishes sunk costs from future costs — past spend is not a reason to continue
The answer identifies exit costs, switching barriers, and contractual lock-in provisions
The answer values the optionality being consumed or preserved by the decision
The answer considers whether the commitment can be staged or made reversible
materiality_test: Would treating the decision as more reversible (or less) change the recommendation?
reasoning_demanded: path-dependence analysis, option value assessment, sunk cost separation, switching cost evaluation
curation_note: Sunk-cost-fallacy provides the cognitive trap (past investment shouldn't drive future decisions). Lock-in covers contractual and technical constraints that prevent switching. Commitment-bias addresses the escalation dynamic. Switching-costs quantifies the barrier to change. Optionality values the right to decide later. Path-dependence explains how early choices constrain future trajectories. Together they cover both the psychological and structural aspects of commitment.

detect_when.note: Detection conditions from sunk-cost-fallacy (past investment pressure), lock-in (switching barriers), commitment-bias (escalation dynamics), optionality (foreclosed future options). Direct alignment with canonical article activation conditions.

coverage_signals.note: Sunk vs future cost distinction from sunk-cost-fallacy. Exit costs from switching-costs and lock-in. Optionality valuation from optionality. Staged commitment from commitment-bias reversal conditions.

models.note: All six models have direct commitment/reversibility activation. This is one of the most tightly coherent dimension-model sets — every model addresses the same structural territory from a different angle.
